data.long_meaning: One who is endowed with knowledge, or possesses wisdom and understanding. Parents who choose Marifat usually hope their child will grow to embody knowledgeable, intelligent and live with faith, good character and purpose.

data.cultural_impact: The name "Marifat" holds a significant cultural impact in the Muslim world, signifying an esteemed level of knowledge or education. It is a title of respect and highlights the importance of knowledge and wisdom in Islamic culture. Marifat can also be associated with its derivatives, such as the term 'Tarifah' which means 'intimate knowledge', emphasizing the value Muslims place on deep understanding and connection to their faith and the world around them. The name "Marifat" embodies the Islamic concept that knowledge and wisdom are central to personal growth, intellectual achievement, and meaningful contribution to society.
data.spiritual_significance: From a spiritual perspective, "Marifat" signifies the acquisition of profound knowledge and understanding of the divine in the Sufi tradition of Islam. This includes the recognition of the ultimate Reality, the attainment of inner knowledge through meaningful experiences, and a deepening bond with the Creator. The pursuit of Marifah, meaning "gnosis" or "spiritual realization," is a significant part of Sufi principles and practices. In this context, the name "Marifat" is an embodiment of the spiritual ideal represented in the famous Islamic verse, "Allah is Beautiful, and He loves beauty" (Quran 55:41), as it represents the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom as a valuable means to connect with the spiritual beauty of the Divine.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Marifat means "knowledge" or "intimate knowledge" in Arabic, symbolizing the quest for spiritual wisdom and understanding in Islam. It represents the journey towards self-realization and enlightenment, emphasizing the importance of learning and seeking knowledge from both the world and the divine.

islamic_reference.note: Traditional Islamic name with deep spiritual significance in Islamic culture

historical_references.reference: Ibn Rushd (Averroes) wrote a work called 'Marifat al-Qur'an', which was a commentary on the Qur'an. It was written in the 12th century during the Almohad Caliphate in Spain. The work was intended to explain the fundamental Islamic doctrines and establish a rational basis for Islamic law.

The Sufi scholar Ibn Arabi wrote a work called 'Fusus al-Hikam', also known as 'Bezels of Wisdom'. This work was completed in 1228 during the Almohad period in Morocco. In the work, Ibn Arabi used the term 'Marifat' to refer to the realization of the inner, esoteric meaning of religious texts and the attainment of gnosis (knowledge of God).
